doc.title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal Interview, 1962-05-24

title: Playing with Claiborne Williams and inviting Donaldsonville people
summary: Allen asks about Claiborne Williams; Edna explains how she met him when her mother invited country people to her wedding.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Oh, we never did hear much about Clayborne Williams from you now. You say you played in his band, did he give you sheet music?
No. No, I didn't play with you.
Oh, you didn't play it then, you just knew it. Oh, no, no, I was too young.

Oh. I was too young. But I played with him. I'll tell you how it was. We were here, as I told you, I was 14 years old when we moved here. And I married when I was 18. So, all the people in the country, we knew, we knew we, instead of sending them an invitation, my mother said, well, we'll make a trip, go out there and invite them. Invite them. So we were going all out in the country, it was different. And everyone was giving us a chicken, a hog, a pig, you know, all that. Oh, we needed, we had to create those things and send them here. So we ended up in Donaldsonville at Clayborne Williams' house. And so my mother, that's how my mother told me, said, well, I know this is Mr. Clayborne Williams. He was my grooms when I got married. Oh, he took such a liking to me. He said, oh, you're a beautiful girl. He says, I'm sorry somebody else is getting you. I said, now listen, Mr. Clayborne, you're old enough to be my grandfather. He said, don't say grandfather, no. And so he joked with me. He said, you play the piano? I said, yes, sir. He says, well, all right. Come on here, let's see how well you can play. And so I started playing. I don't remember the piece I played with. But he got his cornet out, violin. I said, it was just violin. He got his violin out and he played with me. And he played about almost an hour with me. And I didn't miss a note. And I was so nervous playing with a famous man, you know. And so he said, well, you're doing fine. Go on, go on. And so all the old people were talking. And him and I played this piece. He never forgot that. He came later on in years, about two, three, or four years afterwards. I was married and had children then. He says, where's Edna? Where is Edna? The girl who played the piano with me. So my mother sent for me. And I think I had one or two children. He was so happy to see me again. And that's when I played that piano with him and he played the violin. That's the only thought I had of Claiborne William. Of course, I saw him several times after when he visited my mother. She would send for me and I'd come to see him. But I didn't come in no contact with him. And I met his son across the river at Miss Romania. He stopped with Miss Romania. That's my daughter's mother-in-law living in Algiers. He stopped with her a while. And so I went over there visiting my daughter and says, You knew Claiborne Williams from Donaldsonville? I said, yeah. He said, well his son is here. I said, oh I heard of his son but I don't know him. So when he came in, she introduced me to him. That's how I met him. But all those many years I didn't know him. So those are people that my mother knew. Any more?
